title: Care for the image (Leviticus Rabbah 34:3)
hook: Hillel goes to the bathhouse: caring for a body made in God's image is a mitzvah
tomorrow: can it ever be right to change someone's words?

segments.voice: Yesterday, a man drilling under his own seat, and the water coming up for everyone. We're in one boat. Today, the one body you were given to sail it in.
screen: `WE'RE IN ONE BOAT.` → `THE BODY YOU SAIL IN.`

segments.voice: Self-care gets mocked sometimes: face masks, bubble baths, treat yourself. Pampering, not principle. So here's an odd little scene from Leviticus Rabbah. Hillel finishes teaching, and as he walks off, his students follow. Rabbi, where are you going? To do a mitzvah. Which mitzvah? To bathe in the bathhouse. Not a sick visit, not a lesson, not a meal for the poor. A bath. The students stop. That's a mitzvah? Washing up, a commandment? It sounds like a joke. Hillel means it completely.
screen: `PAMPERING, NOT PRINCIPLE?` → `WHERE ARE YOU GOING?` → `TO BATHE. THAT'S A MITZVAH?`

segments.voice: Here's his answer. You know the statues of kings they set up in the theaters and circuses? The man in charge of them scrubs and washes them. He gets paid for it, and he's even honored among the great of the kingdom. And me, created in the image and likeness, as it says, "for in the image of God made He man"? How much more. That's the rabbis' how-much-more argument, kal va-chomer: if the lesser thing deserves care, the greater one deserves more. That solves the puzzle. The Hebrew word is tselem, image. In Hillel's world, an image of the king stood in public, and keeping it clean honored the king. So if a person is an image of God, washing that person isn't vanity. It's upkeep on something royal. The thing to tell a friend tonight: Hillel compared his own body to a statue of the emperor, and won the argument. The same passage has a second scene. Another day Hillel says he's going to do a kindness for a guest in his house. Do you have a guest every day? My poor soul, he says: here today, gone tomorrow. Body as an image, soul as a guest. Both get looked after. Sleep, water, a real meal: not a break from the holy work. Part of it.
screen: `THE STATUES OF KINGS, SCRUBBED.` · `TSELEM: THE IMAGE.` · `UPKEEP ON SOMETHING ROYAL.` · `THE SOUL, A GUEST.` · then, large: `CARE FOR THE IMAGE.`

segments.voice: If you have water nearby, pour a glass, or cup some in your hands. Drink it slowly: notice the cold, the taste, where it goes. Then sit back and let your shoulders drop, the way you'd set down something valuable you've been carrying carelessly all day.
screen: `A GLASS OF WATER.` · `SLOWLY: THE COLD, THE TASTE.` · `SET THE SHOULDERS DOWN.`

segments.voice: Care for the image: Hillel's reason for a trip to the bathhouse. If kings' statues get scrubbed, how much more a body made in the image of God.
Pocket this: care for the image. Hillel walked off to the bathhouse like he was going to synagogue.

howItsDone: Jewish law counts guarding your health as a duty, and teachers often bring Hillel's bathhouse story to show that caring for the body is part of serving God, not a distraction from it.

fork.setup: your friend skips lunch every day to fit in more volunteer shifts. she says eating slowly would be selfish. by Hillel, what do you tell her?
options: 'you're right. serving others always comes before your own body.'
'just grab coffee; it keeps you going without wasting any time.'
'eat lunch. Hillel called a bath a mitzvah; your body is part of the work.'
fork.reveal: for Hillel, caring for a body made in God's image is itself a mitzvah, upkeep on something royal, not time stolen from the holy.

original.note: Hebrew: image, as in 'in the image of God' (Genesis 1:27; 9:6).

chat.meaning: Hillel: if a king's statue gets scrubbed, how much more a body made in God's image. Caring for it is a mitzvah, not a distraction.

notes: Leviticus Rabbah 34:3 paraphrased: Hillel and his students; the statues (ikonin) of kings in theaters and circuses, scoured and washed, the attendant paid and honored among the great of the kingdom; Genesis 9:6. The second scene (the soul as a guest, 'here today, gone tomorrow') is in the same passage; confirm.
Genesis 9:6 quoted from JPS 1917 ('for in the image of God made He man'); confirm.
Gloss 'Hillel: a great early sage' uses 'great', a common honorific; soften to 'an early sage' if a Keeper prefers.
